topics.title: Pencil Grades: H, HB and B
topics.short: H pencils are harder and make lighter lines; B pencils are softer and make darker lines. A bigger number means more of either.
topics.trouble: People think a 6H is darker than a 2H because 6 is bigger. For H pencils a bigger number means harder and lighter; for B pencils, softer and darker.

topics.title: Paper and Erasers
topics.short: Drawing paper has some tooth to grip graphite. A kneaded eraser lifts tone when you press and dab; a vinyl eraser cleans crisp edges.
topics.trouble: People scrub hard with an eraser and rough up the paper. Dab with a kneaded eraser to lighten, and erase gently.

topics.title: Holding the Pencil
topics.short: Hold near the point, as for writing, for small, careful details. Hold farther back or overhand, and move from the elbow, for long, loose lines and broad shading.
topics.trouble: People draw everything with a writing grip and a still wrist, so lines come out short and stiff.

topics.title: Charcoal, Ink and Colored Pencil
topics.short: Charcoal is soft, dark and smudgy; ink is permanent; colored pencil builds color in light layers.
topics.trouble: People expect charcoal to erase cleanly and ink to be fixable. Plan an ink drawing in light pencil first.

topics.title: Line Weight and Line Quality
topics.short: Vary the weight of your lines: heavier for near edges and shadow sides, lighter for far edges and lit sides.
topics.trouble: Every line the same weight makes a drawing look flat, like a page in a coloring book.

topics.title: Contour Drawing
topics.short: A contour line follows the edges of a form slowly, as your eye follows the object, including the edges inside the outline.
topics.trouble: People draw only the outside outline. A contour drawing also follows inner edges: folds, overlaps and where one part meets another.

topics.title: Blind Contour Drawing
topics.short: Draw a contour while looking only at the object, never at the paper. It trains the eye and hand to move together.
topics.trouble: People think a blind contour that looks odd is a failure. Its purpose is slow, careful looking, not a good-looking drawing.

topics.title: Cross-Contour Lines
topics.short: Lines that wrap across a form, like stripes around a ball, show its roundness.
topics.trouble: People draw cross-contour lines straight across a round form, which flattens it. The lines must curve with the surface.

topics.title: Gesture Drawing
topics.short: A gesture drawing takes half a minute to two minutes and catches the movement and weight of a pose, not its details.
topics.trouble: People start a gesture drawing with an outline or a face. Start with one line of action through the whole pose.

topics.title: Positive and Negative Space
topics.short: Positive space is the object; negative space is the space around and between. Drawing the negative shapes helps you see true shapes.
topics.trouble: People ignore the gaps, such as between chair legs or under an arm. Those shapes are easier to judge than the object itself.

topics.title: From Shapes to Forms
topics.short: A shape is flat; a form has depth. A circle becomes a sphere, a square a cube, a triangle a cone and a rectangle a cylinder.
topics.trouble: People use "shape" and "form" as the same word. A shape has height and width; a form also has depth.

topics.title: Drawing a Box
topics.short: Draw the nearest corner first. Edges that are parallel on the box either stay parallel or come together as they go back; they never spread apart.
topics.trouble: People draw the back edges of a box farther apart than the front ones, so the box looks warped.

topics.title: Circles in Depth: Ellipses
topics.short: A circle seen at an angle is an ellipse. It looks thinner near eye level and rounder the farther it is above or below eye level.
topics.trouble: People draw the bottom of a cup as a flat line or give an ellipse pointed ends. Ellipses are smooth all the way around, and the bottom of a cup below eye level is rounder than the top.

topics.title: Building Objects from Forms
topics.short: Break a complicated object into simple forms (boxes, cylinders, spheres and cones), draw those lightly, then refine.
topics.trouble: People draw details first and the overall shape never comes out right. Big forms first, details last.

topics.title: Value and the Value Scale
topics.short: Value is how light or dark a tone is. A value scale steps evenly from white to black, often in 5, 7 or 9 steps.
topics.trouble: People make the light steps too close together and then jump to black. Each step should look as different from its neighbors as every other step.

topics.title: Hatching
topics.short: Parallel lines make tone. Lines closer together, or heavier, read darker.
topics.trouble: People hatch in every direction at once, which looks scribbled. Keep the strokes in one area parallel.

topics.title: Cross-Hatching
topics.short: Layers of hatching that cross at an angle build darker values.
topics.trouble: People cross every area at once, so there is no light left. Add a new layer only where the value should be darker.

topics.title: Stippling
topics.short: Dots make tone: more dots, closer together, read darker.
topics.trouble: People drag the pen and make dashes instead of dots, which changes the texture.

topics.title: Smooth Tone and Blending
topics.short: Build smooth tone with light, even layers of small strokes; a blending stump or tissue can soften it.
topics.trouble: People press hard to get a dark tone fast. Heavy pressure flattens the paper's tooth so later layers won't go on.

topics.title: Contrast and Key
topics.short: High contrast puts very light next to very dark. A high-key picture is mostly light values; a low-key picture is mostly dark.
topics.trouble: People stay in the safe middle grays, so the drawing looks washed out. Use the full range, from white paper to your darkest dark.

topics.title: Where the Light Comes From
topics.short: Choose one light source. Every lit side faces it, and every shadow side and cast shadow points away from it.
topics.trouble: People shade each object on a different side, as if there were several suns.

topics.title: Highlight, Core Shadow and Reflected Light
topics.short: Light on a round form runs highlight, light, halftone, core shadow and reflected light, and the cast shadow lies on the ground beside it.
topics.trouble: People make the reflected light as bright as the lit side. Reflected light is always darker than any value in the light.

topics.title: Cast Shadows
topics.short: A cast shadow falls away from the light. It is darkest and sharpest where the object touches the surface and softens as it goes out.
topics.trouble: People leave a gap between an object and its shadow, so the object seems to float. The shadow touches where the object touches.

topics.title: Shading a Sphere
topics.short: Put the values in order around the ball: highlight, light, halftone, core shadow, reflected light, then the cast shadow.
topics.trouble: People shade a dark ring all around the edge, which makes a flat disc with a dark outline. The core shadow is a band on the side away from the light.

topics.title: Shading a Box: Three Planes
topics.short: Each flat side of a box gets one even value: the side facing the light is lightest and the side turned away is darkest.
topics.trouble: People blend tone across the edges of a box as if it were round. Flat planes change value sharply at the edges.

topics.title: Proportion: Comparing Sizes
topics.short: Proportion is how sizes compare. Choose one part as your unit and measure the rest in it: "the bottle is three caps tall."
topics.trouble: People draw parts at the size they feel they are, a big face and small hands, instead of the size they measure.

topics.title: Sighting with a Pencil
topics.short: Hold the pencil at arm's length with the elbow straight, close one eye, and mark a length with your thumb to compare it with others.
topics.trouble: People bend the elbow between measurements, which changes the scale and makes every comparison wrong.

topics.title: Angles and Plumb Lines
topics.short: Hold the pencil truly vertical or horizontal to judge an edge's angle and to see what lines up above or beside what.
topics.trouble: People tilt the pencil to match the edge instead of holding it level, so there is nothing to compare the angle to.

topics.title: The Grid Method
topics.short: Divide the picture and the paper into matching grids and copy one square at a time. Bigger squares on the paper enlarge the drawing.
topics.trouble: People draw a paper grid with a different shape (ratio) than the picture's grid, which stretches the drawing.

topics.title: Checking Your Drawing
topics.short: Step back, squint to see the big values, and look at the drawing in a mirror to spot crooked or lopsided shapes.
topics.trouble: People keep their nose close to the paper. Many errors only show from a distance or flipped.

topics.title: Showing Depth: Overlap, Size and Placement
topics.short: Things in front overlap things behind; farther things look smaller and, below eye level, sit higher on the page.
topics.trouble: People draw a faraway house the same size as a near one, side by side on one line.

topics.title: The Horizon Line Is Eye Level
topics.short: In perspective, the horizon line is the viewer's eye level. You see the tops of things below it and the bottoms of things above it.
topics.trouble: People think the horizon line is wherever the land happens to end. It is always eye level, even indoors where you can't see the real horizon.

topics.title: One-Point Perspective
topics.short: Facing a box straight on, its edges that go back from you all meet at one vanishing point on the horizon line.
topics.trouble: People let edges that go back miss the vanishing point, or put the vanishing point above or below the horizon line.

topics.title: Roads, Rooms and Rails
topics.short: Roads, railroad tracks, hallways and rooms seen straight on narrow toward one vanishing point, and equal spaces look shorter as they go back.
topics.trouble: People space railroad ties or fence posts evenly on the paper. Equal spaces look closer together as they go back.

topics.title: Two-Point Perspective
topics.short: Turn the box so a corner faces you. Its edges go back to two vanishing points on the horizon, and vertical edges stay vertical.
topics.trouble: People place the two vanishing points close together, which makes boxes look stretched. Put them far apart, even off the page.

topics.title: Three-Point Perspective
topics.short: Looking far up at a tall building or far down from one, the vertical edges also meet, at a third vanishing point above or below.
topics.trouble: People use a third vanishing point for an ordinary eye-level view, where vertical edges should stay vertical.

topics.title: Atmospheric Perspective
topics.short: Faraway things look lighter, bluer, softer and less detailed because of the air between us and them.
topics.trouble: People draw distant hills with the same dark lines and detail as the foreground.

topics.title: The Rule of Thirds
topics.short: Divide the picture into thirds both ways; placing the main subject near one of the lines or crossings often looks livelier than dead center.
topics.trouble: People treat the rule of thirds as a law. It is a guideline; many great pictures put the subject in the center on purpose.

topics.title: The Focal Point
topics.short: The focal point is where the eye goes first. Artists make it with the strongest contrast, the most detail, isolation or lines that lead to it.
topics.trouble: People give every part of a drawing equal detail and contrast, so the eye has nowhere to rest.

topics.title: Balance
topics.short: Symmetrical balance mirrors the two halves; asymmetrical balance offsets a big, quiet shape with a small, strong one; radial balance spreads from a center.
topics.trouble: People think a picture is balanced only when both halves match. Unequal things can balance, like a small dark shape against a large light one.

topics.title: Leading Lines
topics.short: Roads, rivers, fences, gazes and edges lead the eye through a picture, ideally toward the focal point.
topics.trouble: People let a strong line run straight out of the picture and take the viewer's eye with it.

topics.title: Thumbnails and Viewfinders
topics.short: Small quick sketches try out several arrangements and crops before the real drawing; a cardboard viewfinder helps choose the view.
topics.trouble: People start the final drawing at once and discover the composition problems too late.

topics.title: Setting Up a Still Life
topics.short: Group objects of different heights and sizes, overlap some, leave uneven gaps, and light them from one side.
topics.trouble: People line the objects up in a row, evenly spaced and the same height, under a light from straight above.

topics.title: Drawing Texture
topics.short: Texture comes from your marks and the value pattern: short strokes for fur, long ones for wood grain, crisp contrast for rough stone.
topics.trouble: People draw texture evenly everywhere. Show it most where light grazes the surface, and let it fade in shadow and in the distance.

topics.title: Shiny and See-Through Things
topics.short: Shiny things show sharp highlights and reflections with strong contrast; glass shows what is behind it, slightly bent, plus a few bright edges.
topics.trouble: People outline a glass and fill it with gray. Draw what you see through it and on it: shapes, reflections and highlights.

topics.title: Folds in Cloth
topics.short: Cloth hangs from points of support, and folds spread out from them. Shade each fold like a small cylinder.
topics.trouble: People draw folds as random lines. Folds start at a support point (a shoulder, a knee, a hook) and run away from it.

topics.title: Proportions of the Head
topics.short: On an adult head seen from the front, the eyes are about halfway down, the face is about five eyes wide, and the nose ends about halfway from the eyes to the chin.
topics.trouble: People place the eyes too high, leaving too little forehead and skull above them.

topics.title: Drawing Eyes
topics.short: An eye is a ball in a socket: the lids wrap around it, the upper lid casts a shadow on it, and the upper lid covers part of the iris.
topics.trouble: People draw the whole iris as a circle floating in the white, which looks startled.

topics.title: The Nose and Mouth
topics.short: Draw the nose with its planes and shadows rather than a hard outline. The corners of the mouth line up roughly below the pupils.
topics.trouble: People outline the whole nose, so it looks flat and pasted on.

topics.title: Profile and Three-Quarter Views
topics.short: When the head turns, the center line curves around it and the far eye looks narrower; in profile, the ear sits just behind the middle of the head.
topics.trouble: People keep both eyes the same width when the head turns, and put the ear too close to the face in profile.

topics.title: Expressions
topics.short: Eyebrows, eyelids and mouth change together: raised brows and an open mouth for surprise, lowered brows and a tight mouth for anger.
topics.trouble: People change only the mouth. The brows and lids carry much of an expression.

topics.title: Drawing Hands
topics.short: Start with the mitten shape of the palm and fingers together. The middle finger is about as long as the palm, and the knuckles line up on a curve.
topics.trouble: People draw five separate sausages of the same length. Fingers differ in length and the knuckles make an arc.

topics.title: Figure Proportions in Heads
topics.short: Artists measure the body in head heights: an adult is about seven and a half heads tall, and a young child only four or five.
topics.trouble: People draw a child as a small adult. Children have bigger heads for their size and shorter legs.

topics.title: The Line of Action
topics.short: One curved line through the whole pose shows its movement; the head, chest and hips hang on it.
topics.trouble: People draw the body stiff and straight, like a stick figure standing at attention.

topics.title: The Mannequin Figure
topics.short: Build the body from simple forms: an egg for the head, boxes for the chest and hips, cylinders for the limbs and balls at the joints.
topics.trouble: People bend arms and legs between joints. Limbs bend only at the joints: shoulder, elbow, wrist, hip, knee and ankle.

topics.title: The Clothed Figure
topics.short: Draw the gesture and forms first, then hang the clothes on them. Folds pull from the shoulders, elbows, waist and knees.
topics.trouble: People draw the clothes first, and the body underneath comes out the wrong size.

topics.title: Warm-Ups
topics.short: A few minutes of straight lines, circles, ellipses and value scales loosens the hand before a drawing.
topics.trouble: People skip the warm-up and spend the first drawing of the day getting loose.

topics.title: A Sketchbook Habit
topics.short: Short, regular practice adds up: draw a little most days, from life when you can, and date every page.
topics.trouble: People wait for long free afternoons and rarely draw. Ten minutes most days does more.

topics.title: Drawing from Life and from Photos
topics.short: Life drawing shows real depth and light; photos flatten form and can bend near things. Use your own photos or free-to-use ones, and give credit.
topics.trouble: People copy photo distortions (huge near hands, black shadows) as if the eye saw them that way.
